title: Kappa distributions as asymptotic marginals of exponential family ensembles
abstract: Recently (Physica A 660 130370, 2025), emergence of superstatistical behavior in driven classical systems has been shown for systems with constant microcanonical heat capacity. As an application of this result, in this work we show that a system of $N$ particles with inverse gamma distribution of total kinetic energies must have kappa-distributed single-particle velocities in the limit $N \rightarrow \infty$. Our results provide insight into the nature of kappa distributions outside the theory of nonextensive statistical mechanics, while also bringing forward a practical method for the generation of kappa velocities via Monte Carlo Metropolis simulation in the inverse gamma ensemble.
summary: This work shows that the kappa distribution arises naturally as an asymptotic limit when analyzing the single-particle velocity distribution of a system whose total kinetic energy follows an inverse-gamma ensemble. The derivation bypasses reliance on nonextensive statistical mechanics by using standard marginalization techniques in the thermodynamic limit, providing both theoretical insight and a practical Monte Carlo simulation method.
main_problem: To demonstrate that the Kappa distribution emerges naturally as an asymptotic marginal single-particle velocity distribution from a system governed by an inverse-gamma ensemble in the thermodynamic limit.
main_result: The single-particle velocity distribution converges to a kappa distribution form ($P(v|\kappa, 	heta)$) when taking $N 	o \infty$, providing a mechanism for its appearance outside nonextensive statistical mechanics.
method: The derivation involves marginalizing the probability density over the velocities of $N$ particles, starting from an initial exponential family ensemble defined by total kinetic energy constraints.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as $N$ interacting particles whose dynamics are analyzed via steady-state solutions to the Liouville equation. The analysis focuses on the probability density derived from an inverse-gamma distribution of the total kinetic energy.
key_observables: Single-particle velocity distribution $P(v)$, total kinetic energy distribution $P(K)$, and the Kullback-Leibler distance ($	ext{D}_{	ext{KL}}$) used for convergence testing.
important_parameters: The spectral index $\kappa$, ensemble parameters $\gamma$ and $K_0$, and the thermodynamic limit ($N 	o \infty$).
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on taking the thermodynamic limit ($N 	o \infty$) for the asymptotic result, and the initial state is assumed to be an energy steady state.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares simulated histograms of kinetic energy/velocity components against exact inverse-gamma distributions. Figure 2 compares the exact vs. kappa model for kinetic energy and plots $	ext{D}_{	ext{KL}}$ divergence versus $N$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the initial probability density based on total kinetic energy constraints, derives the marginal distribution for total energy ($P(K)$), and then performs a second marginalization over remaining particles to find the single-particle velocity distribution. The final steps involve taking the $N 	o \infty$ limit to map this result onto the known kappa distribution form.
why_interesting: While not directly about quantum systems, the rigorous derivation of non-standard distributions like Kappa from fundamental statistical mechanics principles (marginalization) is highly relevant for understanding generalized thermalization processes in complex many-body systems.
